stem: On a hot, humid afternoon, the nurse at an outdoor event receives four reports. Which client should the nurse see first?

opts.t: A worker with hot skin who is confused and has a core temperature of 40 °C (104 °F)
A spectator who is sweating after walking up the bleachers
opts.w: Sweating after activity is a normal cooling response.

opts.t: A volunteer with cool hands in an air-conditioned tent
opts.w: Skin vessels constricting in a cool space is normal heat conservation.

opts.t: A parent asking which sunscreen to use

why: When heat gain exceeds heat loss, core temperature climbs (hyperthermia). High humidity limits evaporative cooling, so sweating may not be enough. A very high core temperature with confusion shows heat balance has failed. That makes it urgent.
trick: Hot, humid, and confused = the cooling system has lost.
tip: Priority: an unstable vital sign plus a change in mental status comes first.

stem: The nurse checks four IV infusions. Which client needs the nurse first?

opts.t: A client mistakenly receiving plain sterile water through an IV
A client receiving isotonic saline at the prescribed rate
opts.w: Isotonic fluid causes no net change in cell volume.

opts.t: A client asking for a cup of drinking water
opts.w: A routine request that can wait.

opts.t: A client whose IV is due to be changed tomorrow

why: Plain water is extremely hypotonic. In the blood, water rushes into red blood cells, which swell and can burst (hemolysis). An isotonic solution keeps cell volume stable.
trick: Hypotonic = hippo: cells swell, then can pop.
tip: Priority: stop a harmful treatment that is still running before anything else.

stem: On a geriatric unit, which client should the nurse assess first?

opts.t: An 82-year-old who fell, cannot bear weight, and has severe pain in the upper thigh and hip
A 70-year-old with osteoporosis asking about vitamin D
opts.w: Teaching can wait until the possible fracture is assessed.

opts.t: A 75-year-old whose height has decreased slightly over 10 years
opts.w: Gradual height loss from disc compression is expected with aging.

opts.t: A 68-year-old who walks daily and wants to keep doing it
opts.w: A healthy goal, not an urgent problem.

why: Spongy bone weakens sooner than compact bone, and the femoral neck has a lot of it, so hip (upper femur) fractures are common after falls in older adults. A new fall with severe pain and inability to bear weight is acute.
trick: Older adult + fall + can't stand on it = check the hip first.
tip: Priority: a new, acute injury beats chronic, expected changes.

stem: Which client on the neuro unit should the nurse see first?

opts.t: A client with myasthenia gravis who now has trouble swallowing and breathing deeply
A client with tendinitis of the elbow
A client with a healing hamstring strain
A client with Duchenne muscular dystrophy asking about wheelchairs

why: In myasthenia gravis the immune system attacks acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing muscle weakness. When it affects the muscles for swallowing and breathing, airway and breathing are at risk.
trick: Weak NMJ + weak breathing muscles = airway first.
tip: Airway and Breathing outrank everything else.

stem: Four clients have injuries. Which client is at greatest risk for a breathing problem and should be seen first?

opts.t: A client with a high cervical spinal cord injury near the origin of the phrenic nerve
A client with a brachial plexus stretch injury in one arm
opts.w: This affects arm function, not breathing.

opts.t: A client with a sacral nerve injury
opts.w: Sacral nerves serve the lower body, not the diaphragm.

opts.t: A client with numbness in one finger

why: The phrenic nerve, from the cervical plexus, supplies the diaphragm, the main breathing muscle. An injury high in the cervical cord can affect it.
trick: C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive (the phrenic nerve's roots).
tip: Link the nerve to the organ. If the organ is for breathing, that client is the priority.

stem: The nurse receives four calls. Which client needs help first?

opts.t: A client with sudden weakness on one side of the body and slurred speech that started 20 minutes ago
A client with Parkinson disease reporting their usual resting tremor
A client with multiple sclerosis asking about a support group
A client with well-controlled epilepsy requesting a refill

why: Sudden one-sided weakness and slurred speech suggest a stroke: brain injury from blocked blood flow or bleeding. It is acute and time-sensitive, unlike the stable chronic conditions.
trick: Sudden + new neuro deficit = think stroke, act fast.
tip: Priority: sudden new symptoms beat stable, long-term ones.

stem: Which client in the clinic waiting room should the nurse see first?

opts.t: A college student with fever, a severe headache, a stiff neck, and new confusion
A client with a mild tension headache after studying
A client needing a booster vaccine
A client with seasonal allergies

why: Fever, headache, stiff neck, and confusion can signal meningitis, inflammation of the meninges that protect the brain and spinal cord. Infection near the CNS is urgent.
trick: Meninges inflamed + mind changing = urgent.
tip: Any new confusion moves a client up the priority list.

stem: Which skin-color finding should the nurse act on first?

opts.t: New bluish lips and nail beds in a client who is short of breath
Yellowish skin in a client with long-standing, stable liver disease
opts.w: Jaundice from bilirubin is known and stable here.

opts.t: A yellow-orange tint on the palms of a client who eats lots of carrots
Light patches of skin from vitiligo
opts.w: Loss of pigment cells. Not urgent.

why: Cyanosis (a bluish color) reflects poor oxygenation. With shortness of breath, it is a breathing problem. Jaundice, carotene, and vitiligo are pigment changes, not oxygen emergencies.
trick: Blue = Breathing problem.
tip: Priority: a sign tied to oxygen beats color changes from pigment.

stem: A farm clinic nurse has four clients. Which client should be seen first?

opts.t: A worker exposed to a pesticide that blocks acetylcholinesterase, now with muscle twitching and trouble breathing
A worker with a small cut on the hand
A worker with seasonal hay fever
A worker asking about hearing protection

why: Acetylcholinesterase normally breaks down acetylcholine. If it is blocked, ACh builds up and keeps stimulating muscles, which can impair breathing. That is a breathing emergency.
trick: No ACh cleanup = muscles stuck 'on', including the breathing muscles.
tip: Breathing trouble wins priority questions.

stem: Which client in the joint clinic should the nurse see first?

opts.t: A client with a suddenly hot, red, swollen knee and a fever
A client with osteoarthritis and usual morning stiffness
A client with a healing ankle sprain
A client asking about knee braces for running

why: A suddenly hot, swollen joint with fever suggests infection inside the joint cavity. The synovial membrane's phagocytes fight microbes, but an infected joint is acute and can be damaged quickly.
trick: Hot joint + fever = possible infection: see first.
tip: Fever with a new local problem points to infection, which is urgent.

stem: A nurse teaches a client who just started weight training. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

opts.t: "My muscles are sore three days later because lactic acid is still stuck in them."
"Creatine phosphate gives my muscles quick energy for a few seconds."
"I keep breathing hard after a sprint to repay my oxygen debt."
"Lactate can be used again by my body for energy."
opts.w: Accurate. Lactate is a usable intermediate.

why: Lactate is a usable intermediate that is cleared and recycled. Soreness days after unfamiliar exercise is not explained by lactate lingering for days.
trick: Lactate leaves fast. Days-later soreness is something else.
tip: Look for the popular myth. It is often the 'needs teaching' answer.

stem: A nursing student explains IV fluids to a classmate. Which statement shows the student needs more teaching?

opts.t: "A hypotonic solution makes red blood cells shrink."
"A hypertonic solution pulls water out of cells."
"An isotonic solution keeps cell volume about the same."
"Water moves toward the side with more solute that can't cross."

why: Hypotonic solutions make cells SWELL (water enters). Hypertonic solutions make them shrink (crenation). Isotonic solutions keep volume steady.
trick: Hypo = hippo (swells).
tip: One swapped direction is a classic error to catch.

stem: A nurse teaches sun safety at a community fair. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

opts.t: "My darker skin has more melanin, so UV can't damage it at all."
"UV radiation can damage DNA in skin cells."
"Melanin absorbs some UV radiation."
"Skin cancers can come from different kinds of skin cells."
opts.w: Accurate: basal cell, squamous cell, and melanoma differ.

why: Melanin absorbs SOME ultraviolet radiation but doesn't eliminate UV damage. Everyone benefits from sun protection.
trick: Melanin = a shield, not a force field.
tip: Absolute claims ('at all', 'never') usually need correcting.

stem: A nurse teaches a client with a large full-thickness burn. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

opts.t: "My burn will grow new normal skin from the middle on its own, like a scrape."
"This burn destroyed all the layers of my skin."
"Losing this much skin affects my fluid balance and infection risk."
"Good nutrition and blood supply help healing."

why: Full-thickness burns destroy the whole skin and many regenerative structures. Large ones can't simply regrow normal skin from their center the way a superficial wound heals.
trick: Full thickness = full loss of the skin's repair kit.
tip: Match the depth of the injury to how it can heal.

stem: A new nurse is documenting a client's wound location. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

opts.t: "Right and left mean MY right and left as I face the client."
"Directional terms assume the client is in anatomical position."
"The terms still apply even if the client is lying down."
"In anatomical position, the palms face forward."

why: Right and left always refer to the CLIENT'S right and left, which may be on the viewer's left. Directional terms use anatomical position no matter how the client is lying.
trick: It's their body, so it's their right.
tip: Perspective errors are common. Always use the client's view.

stem: A nurse teaches a client with diabetes about carbohydrates. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

opts.t: "My body stores glycogen mostly in my fat tissue."
"Liver glycogen helps keep my blood glucose steady."
"Fiber comes from cellulose that I can't digest."
"Table sugar (sucrose) is glucose joined to fructose."

why: Glycogen is stored mainly in the liver (to support blood glucose) and skeletal muscle (to fuel muscle). Fat tissue stores triglycerides.
trick: Glycogen lives in the Liver and Muscles: 'LM'.
tip: Watch for the right substance in the wrong storage place.

stem: A client asks about fats in the diet. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

opts.t: "Cholesterol has no useful job in my body."
"Phospholipids make up my cell membranes."
"Triglycerides store energy and insulate."
"My body uses cholesterol to make steroid hormones."

why: Cholesterol stabilizes animal cell membranes and is a precursor of steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D-related molecules. Its levels matter for health, but it has essential jobs.
trick: Cholesterol: membranes, hormones, bile, vitamin D. It's not all bad.
tip: 'No useful job' is an absolute. It is usually wrong in physiology.

stem: A nurse teaches a client with a cartilage injury in the knee. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

opts.t: "My cartilage will heal quickly because it has a lot of blood vessels."
"Cartilage heals slowly because it lacks blood vessels."
"Hyaline cartilage covers the ends of my bones in the joint."
"The menisci in my knee are fibrocartilage."

why: Cartilage is avascular, which is part of why it heals slowly. Bone, by contrast, is richly vascular.
trick: No blood vessels = slow repairs.
tip: Two statements that contradict each other: one of them is the answer.

stem: A nurse reviews calcium regulation with a client. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

opts.t: "Calcitonin raises my blood calcium."
"Parathyroid hormone raises my blood calcium."
"Vitamin D helps me absorb calcium from food."
"Osteoclasts release calcium from bone."

why: Calcitonin (from the thyroid) LOWERS blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts and helping osteoblasts deposit calcium in bone. PTH raises it.
trick: CalciTONEin TONES it down. PTH Pulls it up.
tip: Opposing hormones: check which way each one pushes.

stem: A nursing student describes the autonomic nervous system. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

opts.t: "The sympathetic division is the 'rest and digest' system."
"The sympathetic division often raises heart rate during a challenge."
"The parasympathetic division supports digestion and saving energy."
"Both divisions are active in normal daily regulation."

why: Sympathetic = mobilizes resources ('fight or flight'). Parasympathetic = digestion and energy conservation ('rest and digest'). Both work all the time.
trick: Sympathetic = Stress. Parasympathetic = Peace.
tip: Swapped labels are the classic autonomic error.

stem: A 50-year-old client now needs reading glasses. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

opts.t: "Needing reading glasses means I have cataracts."
"With age, my lens has a harder time focusing up close."
"A cataract is a clouding of the lens."
"Glaucoma involves damage to the optic nerve."

why: Presbyopia (reduced near focus with age) and cataract (clouding of the lens) are different processes. Needing reading glasses is presbyopia.
trick: Presbyopia = arms too short to read. Cataract = foggy window.
tip: Similar age-related conditions: match each to its exact change.

stem: A nurse teaches hearing protection to factory workers. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

opts.t: "My middle-ear muscles fully protect me from any sudden loud bang."
"The middle-ear reflex can soften some steady loud sounds."
"Damage to hair cells can cause sensorineural hearing loss."
"Wearing ear protection around loud machines is important."

why: The acoustic (tympanic) reflex tightens middle-ear muscles, but it has a delay and does not reliably protect against sudden loud impulses. Hearing protection is still needed.
trick: The ear's reflex is a slow door. Sudden bangs get in first.
tip: 'Fully' and 'any' signal the false statement.

stem: A student reviews neurotransmitters. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

opts.t: "GABA is the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter."
"Glutamate is a major excitatory transmitter in the CNS."
"Acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine."
"Endorphins help modulate pain."

why: Glutamate is the major excitatory CNS transmitter. GABA is a major INHIBITORY one. Glycine commonly mediates spinal inhibition.
trick: GABA = 'Go Away, Brain Activity' (inhibitory).
tip: Excitatory vs inhibitory pairs are easy to swap. Lock in one.

stem: A client is told a growth is benign. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

opts.t: "Since it's benign, it can never cause any harm."
"A benign tumor doesn't spread to other parts of the body."
"A malignant tumor can invade nearby tissue."
"Where a tumor is located can matter, even if it's benign."

why: A benign tumor stays local and doesn't metastasize, but its location can still make it harmful, for example by pressing on nearby structures.
trick: Benign = stays put, but 'put' can still be a bad spot.
tip: 'Never' and 'any' are red flags.

stem: A client's leg muscles shrank while in a cast for 8 weeks. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

opts.t: "Exercise won't help my muscle come back."
"My muscle shrank because I couldn't use it."
"Disuse reduces the blood vessels and mitochondria in muscle."
"Regular exercise helps keep muscles working as I age."

why: Disuse atrophy shrinks capillary networks, mitochondria, and actin and myosin filaments. Exercise is the best way to rebuild and maintain muscle.
trick: Muscle follows 'use it or lose it', and you can use it to get it back.
tip: A statement that would stop a client from getting better needs correcting.
